visual.text: SHELTER BUDDIES · A PROGRAMME FOR TEENS AGED 14 TO 17
He has been waiting a long time for someone to learn his name.
Give two Sunday mornings a month to a shelter dog or cat that nobody has chosen yet.
A thin brown dog presses its nose through the bars of a kennel. A name card on the gate reads ‘Kopi — here since last year’. A teenager’s hand reaches towards it.

Shelters are full of animals that are fed and safe but rarely touched. Volunteers are few, and the shy ones at the back get the least attention. As a Shelter Buddy, you are matched with one animal for six months. You walk it, brush it, sit beside it, and write a short note after each visit. Those notes help the shelter find it a home.

visual.title: Before you sign up
items: This is not a petting zoo. You will clean kennels and wash bowls.
Some animals will take weeks to trust you.
You need a parent’s consent and closed shoes.
You may not adopt your buddy — but your notes may help someone else to.

visual.text: “For three visits Kopi would not come near me. On the fourth, he fell asleep on my foot. I did not move for an hour.” — Sarah, 16
Apply to be a Shelter Buddy

questions.text: Why does the webpage include the box titled ‘Before you sign up’?

scheme.answer: To make sure readers know that the work is hard and needs patience, so that only teenagers who are serious about it will apply.
accept: To warn teenagers that volunteering involves chores and commitment and is not just playing with animals.

questions.text: Sarah says, ‘I did not move for an hour.’ What does this show about how she felt when Kopi fell asleep on her foot?

scheme.answer: She was so touched that Kopi finally trusted her that she did not want to disturb him.
accept: His trust meant a great deal to her, so she kept still to let him sleep.

questions.text: How does the picture make readers want to help?

scheme.answer: It shows a thin, lonely dog that has been in the shelter for a long time reaching out through the bars, which makes readers feel sorry for it.
accept: The dog pressing its nose through the bars looks as if it is longing for company, so readers pity it and want to be the one to reach out.

questions.text: Look at the headline: ‘He has been waiting a long time for someone to learn his name.’ What does it suggest about the lives of animals in a shelter?

scheme.answer: They are overlooked; nobody gives them personal attention or gets to know them.
accept: The animals are lonely because no one treats them as individuals or spends time with them.
